claims.text: The target material is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
A machine-learning framework can explicitly incorporate microstructural disorder and interstitial-oxygen effects.
The proposed model will agree with conductivity measurements in both the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The proposed model will outperform analytical models based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
The relevant bulk microstructure includes grain boundaries, dislocations, and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen introduced during processing.
Experimental conductivity data and measurements of grain size, defect densities, and oxygen distributions can be used to calibrate the model.
Quantum effects and low carrier scattering dominate conductivity behavior in the nearly 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering and oxygen-induced defect scattering are prominent in the 300–1200 K regime.
The density and distribution of microstructural defects and interstitial oxygen alter electron-scattering rates.
Microstructural defects and interstitial oxygen modify the band structure relative to an ideal defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystal.
Incorporating measured defect types and oxygen-related scattering centers allows the model to adjust effective electron-scattering and band-modification parameters.
Traditional analytical models ignore imperfections that critically influence transport properties.
The model will predict conductivity within ±10–15% of experiment in both specified temperature regimes.
Traditional analytical predictions assume ideal, defect-free single crystals and neglect effects from microstructural imperfections and interstitial oxygen.
The proposed approach is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen levels near 1 wt.% and the stated temperature ranges.
The approach may not extrapolate accurately to substantially higher oxygen concentrations or radically different processing routes that introduce new defect types.
Vacuum sintering can produce nearly fully densified equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a relative density of 99.7 ± 0.2%.
Four-point-probe conductivity measurements over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K provide a measurable benchmark for model evaluation.
Failure to remain within ±15% of measured conductivity across both regimes would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of statistically significant improvement over the traditional analytical model would falsify the hypothesis.
